explanations.explanation: Verse 1 says the crowds came to Him and "He taught them, as was His custom." Crowd shows up, class starts. I wish my habits were that good. Mine is sniffing the oven every ten minutes like it might change its mind.

I get it, I'm a cookie guy, so my first thought is handing out food too. Jesus did feed crowds at other times (Mark 6:41-42). But Mark 10:1 says "He taught them, as was His custom." Same crowd, different moment.
Nothing in this verse sends anybody away. Mark 10:1 says the crowds came to Him and "He taught them, as was His custom." I'd have been hiding behind the cookie rack, but Jesus just teaches.

explanations.answer: Whether it's lawful for a man to divorce his wife
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 2 says they came to test Him, and the question was "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?" Bold move, friend. I won't even argue with my own oven timer.

explanations.answer: Whether it's lawful to pay taxes to Caesar
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because that question really does get asked of Jesus. It comes later, in Mark 12:14. Here in Mark 10:2 the question is about divorce. Different day, different question.

explanations.answer: Whether it's lawful to heal on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: That question shows up in Matthew 12:10, a different passage. Here in Mark 10:2 the Pharisees ask whether it's lawful for a man to divorce his wife. Easy to mix up, since the word "lawful" gets around.

Right. The Pharisees answer that "Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away." (Mark 4 in verse 4, I mean Mark 10:4.) Notice the word they pick is "permitted." Jesus asked what Moses commanded, and that's what they came back with.

Bills are a very grown-up guess, friend. But in Mark 10:4 the Pharisees name a certificate of divorce, not a record of debts. That's the paper Moses permitted a man to write before sending his wife away.

I was bought for a quarter at a closing bakery, so I know a purchase paper when I see one. But Mark 10:4 has the Pharisees naming a certificate of divorce, not a deed. That's what they say Moses permitted a man to write.
Jesus says it Himself: "Moses wrote this commandment for you because of your hardness of heart." (Mark 10:5) That's the reason He gives. Notice He says "for you," talking right to the Pharisees.

explanations.answer: Because the elders asked for it
explanations.explanation: No elders show up in verse 5. Jesus gives one reason: "because of your hardness of heart." Nobody's request gets mentioned, only hearts.

explanations.answer: Because God wanted it that way
explanations.explanation: Thoughtful guess, but that's not the reason Jesus gives. In Mark 10:5 He says Moses wrote it "because of your hardness of heart." Then in verse 6 He goes back to the beginning of creation, and I'll let that speak for itself.

Verse 6 says "from the beginning of creation," and that's as far back as it goes. Jesus skips right past Moses to the very start. I'd get lost going back that far. I need a map to find my own cooling rack.

Noah's days (Genesis 6 to 9) are a good guess for far back, but Jesus doesn't go there. In Mark 10:6 He says "from the beginning of creation," and that's even earlier. He goes all the way to the start.
Abraham's call is in Genesis 12, and that's a long way back. But Jesus goes further. Mark 10:6 says "from the beginning of creation," which is long before Abraham.

Not quite, friend. The quote keeps going: "and the two will become one flesh." Then Jesus adds, "So they are no longer two, but one flesh." (Mark 10:8) So the text says the two become one, not that they stay two separate people.
Right, it's false. The quote says "the two will become one flesh," and Jesus follows it with "So they are no longer two, but one flesh." (Mark 10:8) Two become one, plain as that.
Yes. Jesus says, "Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate." (Mark 10:9) The verse names God as the One who joined them. And it's man who's told not to separate.
Not false, friend. In Mark 10:9 Jesus says, "Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate." God is the One doing the joining. Man is the one told not to separate.

Yes. Verse 10 says that back inside the house, "the disciples asked Jesus about this matter." Asking a follow-up question is smart. I think they wanted to be sure they understood, and I still ask my oven twice after it beeps.
The scribes aren't in this scene at all. Verse 10 says "the disciples asked Jesus about this matter." So it's His own followers asking, back inside the house.
The crowds were around at the start, back in verse 1, but verse 10 changes the scene. Back inside the house, it's the disciples who ask Jesus about this matter. A house only holds so many people.

Yes. Jesus says, "And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery." (Mark 10:12) Verse 11 speaks about a man and verse 12 speaks about a woman. This is a heavy part, and I think it deserves a slow read.

Not false, friend. Verse 12 says, "And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery." Verse 11 speaks about a man, and verse 12 speaks about a woman. This is a heavy part, so take it slowly.
